text: My mother keeps her receipts in shoeboxes, rubber-banded by year and stacked in the hall closet behind the winter coats. As a kid I thought it was madness. Now I read them like a diary: the month the heat stayed on, the week we ate at a restaurant because the car had finally passed inspection. I don’t keep receipts. But I know exactly which closet hers are in.

I failed my driving test twice. The first time I rolled through a stop sign, a small one in a church parking lot, but still. The second time I parallel parked so gently that the examiner asked if I was afraid of the curb. I was. And I passed on the third try, mostly out of spite, and I have been a careful driver ever since.

On Sundays my grandfather made pancakes, and on Sundays they came out wrong: too thick, too pale, one side still raw. He served them with total pride, and we ate them with total loyalty. Years later I followed his recipe to the letter and got the same dense, lopsided stack. I ate all of it.

The summer I turned fifteen I decided to become a person who ran. So I ran, slowly and badly, in my brother’s old sneakers, past the same mailbox every morning until the mailbox and I were on a first-name basis. I never got fast. But by August I could reach the river without stopping, and that was enough to keep going.

There is a particular quiet in our house after an argument. Not angry, exactly; tired. The dishwasher hums, someone’s socks tumble in the dryer, and nobody wants to be first to say something ordinary. I learned to read that quiet early, the way sailors read a sky. Now I can walk into a room and tell within a minute who is ready to apologize.

I keep a list of the bad advice I have been given. Don’t major in English. Never lend books. Always order whatever the waiter recommends. Some of it was kindly meant and some of it was only loud, but I like having the list. Each piece tells me where the person who said it was afraid.

My brother and I shared a bedroom until I was thirteen, and we divided it with a strip of blue tape down the carpet. He crossed it constantly. I never did, and I kept a notebook of his violations. At the time I thought I was defending my territory. I think now I was learning that other people need room too.

When we moved to Ohio I was ten, and I had to learn a new lunch table and a new word for soda. The lunch table took a week. The word never stuck, so I say “pop” in Boston and “soda” back home and get strange looks in both places. Belonging, I have decided, mostly means being wrong in the same direction as everyone around you.

Our dog was terrified of the vacuum. She would lie down in front of it, flat as a rug, and refuse to move, and we always gave in. As a result the living room was never fully vacuumed. But she was never frightened for long, either, and I still think we got the better end of that deal.

I read the last page of a book before the first. People are appalled. But a book whose ending I already know is one I can relax into, the way you relax on a long drive once you are sure the road leads somewhere. What I come for is the sentences along the way.

Grandma’s kitchen smelled of onions, bleach, and the radio, which was always on and always slightly off its station. She sang along to the static as if it were a song she had learned. I used to be embarrassed when friends came over. The house is quiet now, and I would give a great deal to hear her sing it again.

At sixteen I got a job washing dishes at a diner that smelled of burnt coffee. I was bad at it. I broke plates, flooded the floor, and once locked myself in the walk-in freezer, briefly but heroically. The cook, a quiet man named Teo, never raised his voice. He simply handed me a mop each time and showed me where the drain was.

I am afraid of elevators that stop between floors, of phone calls from unknown numbers, and of the second before I press send. My cousin is afraid of birds, specifically pigeons, specifically in groups. We compare notes at holidays, and neither of us has ever convinced the other that our fear is the sillier one.

I used to assume brave people weren’t scared. Then I watched my aunt walk into a courtroom to testify, her hands shaking so hard that the pages rattled. She wore her good blue dress and she did not look at the defendant. She read every word. I have thought about those rattling pages whenever I have had to speak in front of a room.

My town has one stoplight, one diner, and a hardware store that has been going out of business for twenty years. I used to count the days until I could leave. Yet when a stranger on campus eleven hundred miles away asks where I’m from, I say the name slowly, and my voice does something I can’t quite control.

My father taught me to fish, though neither of us caught anything for years. We sat on overturned buckets and watched the water. He told me the same four stories in the same order, and I never mentioned that I had heard them. Lately he tells them less often, and I have started asking for the one about the snapping turtle.

Math was never my subject. In ninth grade it felt like a language everyone else had studied over the summer. Then in eleventh grade a teacher wrote “try again” on a failed quiz instead of a grade, and for the first time I wanted to. I am still slow with fractions. But I can do them, which is different from being unable.

We have a rule at dinner: no phones. My sister broke it first, then my brother, then my father, who kept his under the napkin, and finally my mother, who had made the rule and sat at the head of the table scrolling through recipes. Nobody mentioned it. The rule is still taped to the refrigerator, curling at the corners.

I keep a notebook of words I like. “Petrichor.” “Susurrus.” “Dusk,” which I have loved since I was six for reasons I can’t defend. I rarely use any of them. But on a bad day I read down the page, and the world becomes, briefly, a place with excellent names for rain and shadows.

When I was nine I swore I would never apologize to my sister, and I held out for six years, through two birthdays, a flooded basement, and one disastrous road trip. Then one night over a sink of dishes I said it quietly, and she said, “I know,” and we kept washing. It took me six years to say and about two seconds to hear.
